note: Front lines, occupied areas and arrows are approximate. In the Pacific the shaded areas include sea and show who held the islands, not a front line.
dataNote: Front lines, occupied areas and arrows are approximate reconstructions: the Eastern Front is traced from the US Military Academy-derived campaign maps on Wikimedia Commons, the other theatres by hand from campaign maps and the dates in the cited articles.

chapters.title: Poland overrun
arrows: German Fourth Army cuts the Polish Corridor
German Third Army from East Prussia
German Tenth Army drives on Warsaw
chapters.text: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939 from the west, the north and the south, and Britain and France declared war two days later. German armoured columns took Kraków on 6 September and reached Warsaw within a week. On 17 September the Soviet Union, secretly allied with Germany, invaded from the east; it is not shaded here because it was not yet at war with the Allies. Warsaw surrendered on 28 September and the last Polish troops on 6 October, and Germany and the Soviet Union divided the country along the Bug and San rivers.

chapters.title: Denmark and Norway
arrows: German drive from Oslo to Trondheim
chapters.text: On 9 April 1940 Germany occupied Denmark in a day and landed troops at Norway's main ports, from Oslo to Narvik, to secure the iron-ore route from Sweden. British, French and Polish troops landed to help the Norwegians, and retook Narvik on 28 May. But with France collapsing the Allies withdrew in early June, and Norway's army on the mainland surrendered on 10 June.

chapters.title: The fall of France
arrows: Army Group B into the Netherlands and Belgium
Panzers through the Ardennes to the Channel
chapters.text: On 10 May 1940 Germany invaded the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg. Its main armoured thrust came through the wooded Ardennes, crossed the Meuse at Sedan and reached the Channel at Abbeville on 20 May, trapping the Allied armies in Belgium; more than 330,000 troops were evacuated from Dunkirk. German forces then broke through on the Somme, entered Paris on 14 June, and France signed an armistice on 22 June. Germany occupied the north and the Atlantic coast, while a collaborating French government at Vichy ran the south.

chapters.title: The Battle of Britain
chapters.text: With France beaten, Germany needed control of the air over the Channel before it could invade Britain. From July 1940 the Luftwaffe attacked convoys, ports, airfields and then London, but the Royal Air Force, guided by radar, kept fighting. This was an air battle: no front line moved and no ground changed hands. By the end of October Germany had postponed the invasion indefinitely, though night bombing of British cities, the Blitz, went on until May 1941.

chapters.title: The desert war
chapters.text: Italy invaded Egypt in September 1940 but stopped at Sidi Barrani; a British counter-attack in December drove the Italians back across Cyrenaica and captured about 130,000 prisoners. German troops under Rommel arrived in 1941 and pushed the British back to Egypt, though besieged Tobruk held out for eight months. The front swung back and forth along the coast until, in June 1942, Rommel won at Gazala, took Tobruk on 21 June and advanced into Egypt as far as El Alamein.

chapters.title: Greece, Yugoslavia and Crete
arrows: German drive from Bulgaria to Athens
chapters.text: Italy invaded Greece from Albania on 28 October 1940, but the Greeks threw it back and advanced deep into Albania. On 6 April 1941 Germany, with Italy, Hungary and Bulgaria, attacked Yugoslavia and Greece; Belgrade fell on 12–13 April and Yugoslavia surrendered on 17 April. German forces entered Athens on 27 April as British and Commonwealth troops were evacuated, and an airborne invasion took the island of Crete by 1 June.

chapters.title: Barbarossa and the Battle of Moscow
chapters.text: On 22 June 1941 Germany and its allies invaded the Soviet Union with more than three million troops. They encircled huge Soviet armies at Minsk, Smolensk and Kiev, where over 600,000 men were lost in September, and by early September had cut Leningrad off by land. The drive on Moscow in October and November reached the outskirts of the city, but in December the Red Army counter-attacked in the snow and pushed the exhausted Germans back.

chapters.title: Pearl Harbor and Japan's sweep
arrows: Japanese conquest of the Dutch East Indies
chapters.text: On 7 December 1941 Japan attacked the US fleet at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii, far to the east of this map, and on the same day began invading the Western colonies in South-East Asia; it had been at war with China since 1937. Hong Kong fell on 25 December, Manila on 2 January and Singapore, with about 80,000 British and Commonwealth troops, on 15 February. By May 1942 Japan held Malaya, the Dutch East Indies, the Philippines and Burma, and its navy was checked only in the Coral Sea in early May.

chapters.title: Midway, Papua and Guadalcanal
arrows: Japanese advance on the Kokoda Track
Australian advance to Buna and Gona
chapters.text: At Midway, in the central Pacific far north-east of this map, US aircraft sank four Japanese carriers on 4 June 1942 and ended Japan's run of victories. In August US Marines landed on Guadalcanal and held its airfield through six months of land, sea and air battles until Japan withdrew in February 1943. In Papua, Australian troops stopped a Japanese overland advance on Port Moresby along the Kokoda Track and, with US forces, retook the Buna and Gona beachheads by January 1943.

chapters.title: Stalingrad
arrows: Case Blue: Army Group B to Stalingrad
Army Group A into the Caucasus
chapters.text: In summer 1942 Germany attacked in the south, aiming for the Caucasus oilfields and the city of Stalingrad on the Volga. Its armies reached the Caucasus mountains and fought their way into most of Stalingrad. On 19 November the Red Army struck the Romanian armies on both flanks and four days later encircled the German Sixth Army in the city. Relief attempts failed, and the last German troops in Stalingrad surrendered on 2 February 1943, the war's most famous turning point.

chapters.title: El Alamein to Tunis
arrows: Eighth Army's pursuit from El Alamein to Tripoli
Allied advance from Algiers into Tunisia
chapters.text: On 23 October 1942 Montgomery's Eighth Army attacked at El Alamein and after twelve days broke through; Rommel retreated more than 2,000 km, losing Tobruk, Benghazi and, on 23 January 1943, Tripoli. On 8 November American and British troops landed in Morocco and Algeria (Operation Torch), and the Vichy French forces there soon joined the Allies. German and Italian troops held Tunisia through the winter and struck back at Kasserine in February, but Tunis fell on 7 May and the last Axis forces in Africa surrendered on 13 May.

chapters.title: Kursk and the Dnieper
arrows: Soviet counter-offensives at Orel and Kharkov
Soviet advance to the Dnieper and Kiev
chapters.text: In July 1943 Germany attacked the Soviet bulge around Kursk from north and south, but the Red Army had built deep defences and stopped both thrusts within a week. Soviet counter-offensives then retook Orel and, on 23 August, Kharkov. Germany never again launched a major offensive in the East. By the end of the year the Red Army had liberated Smolensk, crossed the Dnieper and retaken Kiev on 6 November.

chapters.title: Sicily and Italy
arrows: Seventh Army from Gela to Palermo and Messina
Eighth Army up the east coast of Sicily
chapters.text: Allied armies invaded Sicily on 10 July 1943; Mussolini was overthrown, and on 8 September Italy surrendered as the Allies landed on the mainland. German troops seized the north and centre of Italy and held a series of defensive lines across the mountains, above all at Monte Cassino through the winter of 1943–44. Rome fell on 4 June 1944, but the Germans then held the Gothic Line in the northern Apennines until the spring of 1945. After a final Allied offensive took Bologna and crossed the Po, the German armies in Italy surrendered on 2 May 1945.

chapters.title: Island-hopping and the Philippines
chapters.text: From November 1943 US forces advanced across the central Pacific by seizing key islands for airfields and bypassing others: Tarawa in the Gilberts, Kwajalein and Eniwetok in the Marshalls, then Saipan and Guam in the Marianas in summer 1944, from where B-29 bombers could reach Japan. In October 1944 US troops landed on Leyte in the Philippines, and the Battle of Leyte Gulf destroyed most of what remained of the Japanese navy. Manila was retaken in March 1945 after a month of fighting that killed about 100,000 civilians, and Iwo Jima was taken the same month at a heavy cost.

chapters.title: D-Day and the liberation of France
arrows: Advance to Belgium and the German border
chapters.text: On 6 June 1944 more than 150,000 American, British, Canadian and other Allied troops landed on the beaches of Normandy. For seven weeks they fought slowly through the hedgerows, taking Cherbourg and Caen, until American forces broke out at Saint-Lô at the end of July. The German armies in Normandy were largely destroyed around Falaise, Paris was liberated on 25 August, and a second landing in southern France on 15 August drove north up the Rhône. By mid-September the Allies had liberated most of France and Belgium and reached the German border.

chapters.title: Bagration
chapters.text: On 22 June 1944, three years after the German invasion, the Red Army attacked German Army Group Centre in Belorussia. Within two weeks it had encircled much of the army group and freed Minsk on 3 July, and by August it had advanced some 500 km to the Vistula and the edge of East Prussia. In Warsaw the Polish Home Army rose against the Germans on 1 August, but the uprising was crushed by October. In late August a new offensive broke the front in Romania, which changed sides on 23 August; Soviet troops entered Bucharest on 31 August.

chapters.title: From the Bulge to Berlin
chapters.text: Germany's last offensive in the West, through the Ardennes in December 1944, made a deep 'bulge' in the American lines but was stopped short of the Meuse. In January 1945 the Red Army swept from the Vistula to the Oder, 70 km from Berlin, while the Western Allies cleared the Rhineland and crossed the Rhine in March. American and Soviet troops met on the Elbe at Torgau on 25 April, as Soviet armies fought their way into Berlin, which surrendered on 2 May. Germany surrendered unconditionally on 7–8 May 1945.

chapters.title: Okinawa, the atomic bombs and Japan's surrender
arrows: Soviet invasion of Manchuria: western front
Soviet invasion of Manchuria: eastern front
chapters.text: US forces landed on Okinawa on 1 April 1945 and took the island by late June in one of the bloodiest battles of the Pacific war, in which a large share of the island's civilians died. On 6 August the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, and on 9 August a second on Nagasaki; the same day the Soviet Union declared war and invaded Manchuria. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August and signed it aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945.
